Unwilling to accept Reb Avraham’s hospitality, but also too uncomfortable turning him down, Baruch found it easier to just leave Liozna entirely.

Avraham gave Baruch the desire to study with Reb Avraham’s own teacher: Reb Avraham Ze’ev. And so, once Baruch was already

leaving town, he decided to set out for Beshenkovitch.

passed through Dobromysl, and, as Reb Avraham had mentioned, it was almost Pesach. The only home in the world in which Baruch would feel comfortable spending the Yom Tov was the home of his friend, Eliezer Reuven. And so, Baruch decided to stop there along the way.

When Baruch arrived at the smithy, it looked just the way it did when he was last there. The stone-covered walls, smoke-tinted

windows, and timeworn, billowing chimney filled Baruch’s heart with a familiar warmth. Already from a few feet away, you could hear the telltale sounds of Eliezer Reuven at work: frequent hammer bangs, the crackling fire, and Eliezer Reuven’s steady chant: “Lamna- tzei-ach, miz-mor, l’Dovid…”

Baruch knocked gently on the door, and pushed it open. Inside, Eliezer Reuven was hard at work

LAST TIME: Baruch correctly predicts the count’s children’s visit, so he avoids the hut, and soon returns to the beis hamidrash. Reb Avraham becomes his chavrusa. They learn together all winter, but after Reb Avraham invites Baruch for Pesach, he finds that Baruch has disappeared once again. Back to Dobromysl

Eliezer Reuven washed his hands and gave Baruch a hearty shake. Shmuel Nachum smiled and greeted Baruch, too. The teenager’s shoulders were slumped, though, and the smile didn’t reach his eyes.

daughters are doing wonderfully. The first two have gotten married, Baruch Hashem, both to talmidei chachamim. And the third, she is still a bit young.” Then, Eliezer Reuven’s smile drooped. In a lowered voice, he said. “My Shmuel Nachum, on the other hand…”

It was as if Eliezer Reuven didn’t even hear Baruch. “I tried everything. Everything! I hired the best melamed. It didn’t help. I even asked the rav of the town for advice. But after he didn’t show … success … the rav himself told me it would be best to teach him a trade. ”

Eliezer Reuven sighed. “That’s what the rav said, too.”

Baruch sat down and spoke with Eliezer Reuven for a few more minutes. He asked about coming for the Yom Tov meals, which of course Eliezer Reuven happily agreed to. Baruch paid for his meals on the spot.

Whenever Eliezer Reuven heard Baruch and his sons-in-law learning or discussing Torah, he would hurry over and pull up a stool. He didn’t understand much—certainly not enough to contribute—but his face would light up just from listening in.

Shmuel Nachum, too, would often come and listen, but he set his stool further back than his father’s; he always sat apart from the group. When Shmuel Nachum listened, his eyes would appear downcast. Every so often, he would chew on his lip.
